body:
I counted three farms on the driver's usual loop. The first two took the pale sacks and each called about sick animals. The third refused the load because its storage room was full.

He was annoyed about bringing half his cargo home. I remember that because he made me sign for the return before he'd carry in my flour.
title: The route on the feed bill

body:
I drove the field worker to town after his boots split. He had come from the treated rows that morning. He shivered in my car while my sister, who had worked the covered greenhouse, complained only about the heat.

We bought a cheap pair of boots and left the old ones wrapped in newspaper. I never finished paying her back for the fuel.
title: The boots in the passenger seat

body:
The first house took drinking water from a barrel beside the sprayed field. The next house had a covered well and said its children were eating normally.

I carried the same groceries to both doors. The bread went stale at the first one because nobody wanted it.
title: Two stops past the mill

body:
The truck carried bagged seed on Monday, then produce on Tuesday without washing the bed. Green dust was still in the corners where the produce crates sat.

I helped unload and found the dust on my cuffs. It was easier to make a joke about the driver's housekeeping than to ask him to turn around.
title: The load that crossed the bridge

body:
One stop on my route turned back the replacement feed because there was no room for it. That man's animals were still feeding when the others stopped drinking.

His wife told me not to treat this as good luck. I wrote the dates on a grocery list in case I forgot which week the truck had gone through.
title: The farmer who kept his old stock

body:
I lent our shovel across the fence after we dug the treated drainage ditch. Their field had not been sprayed. They returned it with the same pale clay on its blade and said their dog had been digging there.

I meant to scrub it before the children used it in the garden. It stayed by the door while the ordinary chores piled up.
title: The shared shovel

body:
The boxes of greens came in with gritty water underneath. The dry boxes delivered an hour earlier stayed crisp; these left soft stems and the same green mark on my hands.

I put them on separate shelves. The receipt printer was broken, so I wrote the difference on the back of my own shopping list.
title: The wet market boxes

body:
The second farm borrowed the trailer after the feed run. No one rinsed the corners. Two days later they called about the young goats, though their own feed had not changed.

I had wanted to lend them a clean blanket too, but there was only room for the trailer and a sack of bedding.
title: The trailer at dusk

body:
Rain got through the canvas at the front of the load. The wet bags came apart; the dry bags at the back held their shape. The wet grain went out to the pens first.

I put a mark on my pocket list so I'd remember which pen got which. It felt petty to count sacks while the animals refused breakfast.
title: The sacks under the canvas

body:
I took the field crew home in two trips. The crew who sprayed the south rows looked tired before sundown. The crew who repaired the fence away from those rows argued about pay all the way back.

They shared a truck and the same sandwiches. I wrote their tasks down on the back of a fuel receipt because the faces were beginning to blur.
title: The worker on the return trip
